content: 1. Sarkar et al. (2016) conducted a cross-sectional, mixed-method study in rural India to evaluate the feasibility of supervised self-testing for HIV using an oral fluid-based rapid testing method among pregnant women. The study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 2. Strauss et al. (2018) explored the stated and revealed preferences for HIV testing among truck drivers in Kenya, assessing whether oral self-testing could increase testing uptake. Their findings were published in BMC Public Health. 3. Brown et al. (2016) investigated the information, motivation, and behavioral skills of high-risk young adults regarding the use of HIV self-tests. The study was published in AIDS and Behavior. 4. Lippman et al. (2018) reported high acceptability and increased frequency of HIV testing among South African men who have sex with men (MSM) following the introduction of HIV self-testing and network distribution. The study appeared in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 5. Marley et al. (2014) examined the introduction of rapid oral-fluid HIV testing among high-risk populations in Shandong, China, highlighting its feasibility and challenges. The study was published in BMC Public Health. 6. Matovu et al. (2017) conducted a qualitative study in Uganda to understand the perceptions of pregnant women and their male partners regarding female partner-delivered HIV self-testing. The study was published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 7. Schnall et al. (2016) used a think-aloud study to observe whether high-risk young adults appropriately use HIV self-tests. Their findings were published in AIDS and Behavior. 8. Zhong et al. (2017) assessed the acceptability and feasibility of a social entrepreneurship testing model to promote HIV self-testing and linkage to care among men who have sex with men. The study was published in HIV Medicine. 9. Grimsrud et al. (2023) discussed the future of HIV testing in eastern and southern Africa, emphasizing broader scope and targeted services. The study was published in PLOS Medicine. 10. WHO guidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention were accessed on October 9, 2023, providing recommendations for its implementation. 11. The integration of HIV testing and linkage into family planning and contraception services was detailed in an implementation brief accessed on October 9, 2023. 12. Ong et al. (2022) conducted a systematic review of risk-based screening tools to optimize HIV testing services. The study was published in Current HIV/AIDS Reports. 13. Lubega et al. (2024) analyzed secondary program data to evaluate the performance of an adolescent and adult HIV risk screening tool in Uganda, highlighting its potential to miss HIV-positive individuals. The study was published in Tropical Medicine and Infectious Disease. 14. Schaefer et al. (2021) conducted a global summary and forecasting study on the adoption and use of oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) guidelines. The study was published in The Lancet HIV. 15. Mayer et al. (2020) reviewed barriers to the wider use of PrEP in the United States, providing a narrative analysis. The study was published in Advances in Therapy. 16. Muhumuza et al. (2021) explored perceived barriers and facilitators of PrEP uptake among young people in Uganda, Zimbabwe, and South Africa. The study was published in the Archives of Sexual Behavior. 17. Patel et al. (2016) examined facilitators and barriers to PrEP use in heterosexual HIV serodiscordant couples in Kisumu, Kenya. The study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 18. Mack et al. (2014) consulted community stakeholders in Kenya to identify barriers and facilitators to PrEP eligibility screening and ongoing HIV testing among target populations. The study was published in BMC Health Services Research. 19. Ortblad et al. (2020) designed a care pathway for pharmacy-based PrEP delivery in Kenya, based on collaborative stakeholder consultations. The study was published in BMC Health Services Research. 20. Kiptiness et al. (2022) conducted a systematic literature review on the use of HIV self-testing to support PrEP delivery. The study was published in Current HIV/AIDS Reports. 21. Cox et al. (2024) modeled the impact of scaling up HIV self-testing for oral PrEP on drug resistance and HIV outcomes in western Kenya. The study was published in The Lancet HIV. 22. Carballo-Diéguez et al. (2012) investigated whether gay and bisexual men at high risk of HIV infection would use over-the-counter rapid HIV tests to screen sexual partners. The study was published in the Journal of Sex Research. 23. Pant Pai et al. (2017) conducted a cross-sectional survey to understand key stakeholders' perspectives on HIV self-testing in Canada. The study was published in AIDS and Behavior. 24. Witzel et al. (2017) conducted a qualitative study in England to explore barriers, facilitators, and anticipated impacts of implementing HIV self-testing. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 25. Witzel et al. (2019) piloted an internet-based randomized controlled trial of HIV self-testing targeting MSM and transgender individuals in England and Wales, focusing on advertising strategies and intervention acceptability. The study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases. 26. Updated guidelines on self-administration of injectable contraception were accessed on October 9, 2023. 27. A sexual and reproductive health self-care measurement tool was accessed online on October 9, 2023. 28. Consolidated guidelines on person-centered HIV strategic information, emphasizing the strengthening of routine data for impact, were accessed on October 9, 2023. 29. WHO recommends prioritizing populations most affected by HIV and at high ongoing risk of infection, including key populations and their partners, men, adolescents, young people, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and other vulnerable groups. Tailored HIV testing services should address the specific needs and preferences of these populations. 30. Key populations, such as men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals, are at higher ongoing risk of HIV infection and require targeted HIV testing, prevention, and care services. 31. Men with HIV are less likely to access testing and care services than women, necessitating the design of HIV testing approaches specifically for men. 32. Adolescents and young people remain vulnerable to HIV and are less likely to test than adults, particularly in high HIV burden settings. Programs should prioritize adolescent-friendly approaches and integrate HIV testing into sexual and reproductive health services. 33. Pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B at least once during pregnancy, preferably in the first trimester. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid testing is recommended in antenatal care settings. 34. Infants and children exposed to HIV should receive virological testing as early as possible to enable immediate initiation of antiretroviral therapy for HIV-positive infants. 35. Network-based testing services, including self-testing, should be offered to contacts and partners of people with HIV to expand testing and prevention efforts. 36. Integrated testing services for HIV, viral hepatitis, and STIs should be made available to migrants, refugees, and displaced populations in high HIV burden settings. 37. Tailored HIV services should address the needs of other vulnerable populations, such as truck drivers, uniformed service personnel, fisherfolk, and indigenous people, based on local epidemiology and context.
